summary:
Legal gender recognition in Denmark has operated by self-declaration since 1 September 2014. A person over 18 states the wish to change registered sex and completes a six-month reflection period; no medical evaluation, psychiatric diagnosis, surgery or sterilisation is required. Parliament removed the diagnosis and surgery requirements in June 2014 by 59 votes to 52. Those requirements dated to the Act on Sterilisation and Castration of June 1929, one of the first gender-change laws in the world, which had made irreversible sterilisation a condition of the process.

Danish passports are issued with male, female and X sex descriptors, so a non-binary traveller can carry a travel document that records neither male nor female.

Gender identity is not a ground for arrest or prosecution. The F&M Global Barometers country profile records that freedom from gender-identity-based arbitrary arrest was affirmed in every year from 2011 to 2024. Same-sex sexual activity was decriminalised by the Penal Code of 1930, in force from 1933, and the age of consent has been 15 regardless of sexual orientation or gender since 1977.

Denmark removed gender identity disorder from the National Board of Health's list of mental illnesses in 2016, effective 1 January 2017, the second country to do so after France in 2010. In May 2016 the government stated it would act unilaterally by October 2016 if the World Health Organization did not remove the classification; the WHO replaced the diagnosis with gender incongruence, reclassified as a sexual health condition, in June 2018.

Discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression and sex characteristics is prohibited in Danish law, but the statutory text is uneven. The 1996 Act on Prohibition of Unequal Treatment in the Labor Market lists sexual orientation and does not explicitly name gender identity or expression. A 2015 ruling by the Aarhus court, in a case brought by a transgender woman against a staffing agency, held that her clothing and appearance were the sole reason for her dismissal and that both the Equal Treatment Act and the Anti-Discrimination Act covered it, awarding DKK 30,000 in compensation against Jysk Mandskabsservice while acquitting the client company for insufficient proof. That judgment, the first on trans discrimination in Denmark, extended protection to gender identity and gender expression despite the absence of explicit wording. Complaints are considered by the Board of Equal Treatment, established under the 2008 Act on the Board of Equal Treatment. F&M records workplace anti-discrimination law covering gender identity since 2015, and fair-housing protection on the same ground throughout the period it measures.

Hate-crime provision is narrower than the discrimination framework. Penal Code amendments adopted in 2004 add penalties for crimes committed because of a person's sexual orientation; gender identity is not named in that provision.

Access to trans health care has tightened since 2023. Guidelines issued that year recommend puberty blockers at Tanner stage two or three, described as buying time for further exploration. Children under ten showing adequate signs of gender dysphoria trigger advisory information for parents. Children over ten face at least five investigative interviews, a psychiatric evaluation, informational sessions on hormone therapy and review of school and municipal records. Hormone treatment can be consented to from age 15 without parental involvement, and no surgical options are available before 18. Assessed barriers include psychosis and autism where dysphoria is treated as an aspect of mental illness, and a history of abuse, self-harm or suicidal ideation. Adult waiting times run about 11 to 16 months for hormone therapy and four to six years for bottom surgery, and many trans adults in Denmark seek care abroad. Patients report being required to present in ways matching stereotypical gender roles in order to obtain hormone therapy.

The Supreme Court ruled on 10 September 2024 that it is not a violation of human rights for a transgender inmate to serve in a men's prison department. That judgment is the leading Danish authority on the placement of trans people in custody.

Denmark granted asylum to a transgender woman from Guatemala in 2013, the first such grant, after accepting that return would expose her to police attacks and threats over her trans activism. She was initially refused, and the case was reopened once she demonstrated that her life would be in danger on return. She was placed in a facility for men, where she was sexually assaulted several times.

A migrant transgender woman was murdered in a hotel room in Copenhagen in July 2024, as recorded in ILGA-Europe's 2025 annual review.

Partner recognition is long established. Registered partnerships were created by a law enacted on 7 June 1989 and in force from 1 October 1989, the world's first such law, with new registrations closed on 15 June 2012. Marriage between people of the same sex has been legal since 15 June 2012, following a government bill introduced on 14 March 2012 that passed by 85 votes to 24 on 7 June and received royal assent five days later; the gender-neutral law covers marriages in the Church of Denmark.

Social climate data is mixed. The Danish Institute for Human Rights LGBT+ barometer records that 38% of homosexual and bisexual respondents report differential treatment based on gender, sexual orientation or appearance, and that hate speech targeting sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, or sex characteristics recurs annually. Under the UN Committee Against Torture's eighth periodic review, some trans people, QTIBIPOCs and migrants reported denial of access to spaces and services and threats, and anti-trans discourse intensified while Parliament debated lowering the age limit for legal gender recognition; the committee urged access to psychosocial counselling and a remedy for intersex people. Denmark signed a United Nations resolution against intersex discrimination in March, recorded in the 2025 annual review.
tangentialFactors:
Denmark's legal framework is rated among the strongest in the world for LGBTQ+ people, and the 2014 self-identification law is credited by activists with cooling the national debate over trans rights.

Family recognition continues to widen. In August 2024 the government announced a plan to strengthen legal recognition of families with three or four parents, a step adjacent to the partner and parent recognition already in force.
localsOnly:
Openly transgender people serve without hindrance in all branches of the Danish Defence, and discrimination is prohibited in recruitment, placement and promotion. A 2019 report found 69% of LGBT respondents were open about their sexual orientation to colleagues and 9% felt unable to be.

The Danish Institute for Human Rights and ILGA-Europe record that 40% of LGBTI students aged 15 to 25 reported self-harm in the past year, two to three times the rate among their classmates.

Joint adoption has been permitted since 1 July 2010, following stepchild adoption from 1999. Parliament voted on 2 June 2006 to allow lesbian couples access to artificial insemination, and since 2013 the non-biological parent is entered on the birth certificate as the other natural parent for in vitro fertilisation. Gay and bisexual men have been able to donate blood since March 2020 on condition of no sex in the preceding four months, with a waiver for stable monogamous relationships; the rule was amended in July 2024 to remove the distinction between heterosexual and homosexual anal sex.

No conversion-therapy ban is in force in Denmark; a bill was revived in August 2026.
